TS039-020----:
On a W-facing slope of rising ground in mountainous region overlooking Aughvaria river valley to the W with good views from SSE through W to N and overlooking a nearby wedge tomb (TS039-021----) c. 100m to the SW. A well-preserved gallery (L c. 3.7m; Wth 1.2m at W; 0.86m to E) aligned E-W; represented by two sidestones to the N and S with evidence of several outer-wall stones on the N and S sides. The E end of the gallery is either missing or grass covered. Two roofstones (dims. 1.7m x 0.9m x 0.35m; 1.9m x 1.5m x 0.4m) survive over the gallery. There is a septal stone (dims. 1.4m x 0.22m) at the W end of the chamber (L 2.4m; Wth 0.8m) which is proceeded by a portico (L 0.9m; Wth 1.2m). (De Valera & Ó Nualláin 1982, vol.4, 92-3; Borlase 1897, 53-4).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
TS039-021----:
On a W-facing slope of rising ground in a mountainous region overlooking the Aughvaria river valley to the W, with a wedge tomb (TS039-020----) c. 100m to the NE. The well-preserved gallery (L. c. 3.25m; Wth 1.1m to W, 0.86m to E) opens to the W and is aligned E-W; represented by two sidestones to the N and S with possible evidence of outer-wall stones on the N and S sides. Two roofstones (dims. 1.4m x 1.9m x 0.3m; 1.9m x 1.7m x 0.35m) survive over the gallery. A septal stone (dims. 1.4m x 0.22m) at the W end of the gallery divides the chamber from the portico (L 1.3m; int. Wth 1.25m; ext. wth 2m). A field boundary intersects the outer walling at the N and S with possible remains of an earthen mound resting on top of the roofstones. (De Valera & Ó Nualláin, 1982, vol.4, 93-4; Borlase 1897, 53-4)
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
TS039-053----:
On top of a small rounded hillock in upland area. There are good views in all directions, especially of the Galtee Mountains to the S. Up to c. 2005 there was a small low standing stone atop this hillock. Between 2005 and 2006 it was removed and is no longer visible. In places the hillock appears to have been artificially constructed, however, in other places it appears to be natural. Depicted as a small quarry on the 1st (1840) ed. OS 6-inch map and as a hollow (dims. c. 18m N-S; c. 15m E-W) on the 1902-03 revision. The standing stone may have been marking a burial mound, which is possibly the low hillock that still survives.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 23 March 2015
TS044-001----:
On a poorly drained S-facing slope of Knockastanna Hill overlooking Gortnageragh river valley in upland region. Poorly preserved remains consisting of three stones, two of which are prostrate (dims. 0.98m x 1.15m x 0.8m; 1.34m x 1m x 0.13m) and one orthostat (dims. H 0.75m; L 0.95m; T 0.20m) located to the SW of the former stones. Possibly the remains of a poorly preserved wedge tomb orientated on an E-W axis. Described by Crawford (1910, 41) as a 'destroyed dolmen, consisting of three stones, two of which are side by side, one pointed with the third stone located 8 feet [2.4m] distant in the same line'. Classified by De Valera and Ó Nualláin as a possible wedge tomb consisting of a single orthostat and two superimposed slabs based on the description of the tomb in the OS letters (1982, 94-5) where it is described as a tomb orientated 'east and west; it was ten feet [3m] in length and three feet eight inches [5.1m] in breadth but only four stones of it are now standing; the one on the south side is six feet [1.8m] long; four feet [1.2m] high at the west end and two feet [0.6m] at the east end, and one foot six inches [0.4m] high; the one forming the west end is six feet [1.8m] long, three feet three inches [1.6m] high and one foot thick [0.3m]; and the one at the north is three feet [0.9m] long, one foot six inches [0.4m] high and one foot [0.3m] in thickness. The flag supported by these inclines towards the east measures five feet two inches [1.57m] from north to south and four feet six inches [1.36m] from east to west and eight inches in thickness (ibid.).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
TS045-001002-:
On a gentle SW-facing slope of rising ground, in upland region overlooking the Gortnageragh river valley. There is a ring-cairn (TS045-001001-) immediately to the S. A standing stone (0.45m x 0.23m; H 0.45m) rectangular in plan and orientated E-W. Though low in height, it is likely that this is the stone which is depicted on the 1903 revision of the OS 6-inch map as a 'Pillar Stone'.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS045-002----:
On a gentle SE-facing slope of rising ground in an upland area. There are good views in all directions. A ring-barrow (TS045-010----) lies c. 550m to the SSE. The stone is incorporated in the S face of a townland boundary running NW-SE. A limestone triangular-shaped stone (1.25m x 0.13m; H 2.1m) orientated N-S. The broad faces of the standing stone taper on both sides to an apex with traces of natural hollows on the surface which may be the result of natural erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS045-009----:
On top of heather covered hill in mountainous region with good panoramic views in all directions. Poorly preserved monument partially covered in heather and bog consisting of a low circular rise (diam. N-S 7m; H 0.6m) of heather covered bog with single large recumbent large slab (dims. L 1.9m x H 0.5m x T 0.4m) orientated on a NW-SE axis visible in centre of low mound. This low orthostat is described by DeValera & Ó Nualláin as a possible septal stone of a wedge tomb (De Valera, R. & Ó Nualláin, S, 1982, vol.4, 99). Described by Crawford (1910m 46) as an almost destroyed monument of which "only the dividing stone remains in position; it is 6 feet 9 inches [2m] long, and 1 foot 9 inches [0.48m] high and wide. Three other stones are lying loose, each about 3 feet [0.9m] by 2 feet [0.6m]".
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS052-050----:
On high ground, in grassland. There are good views in all directions. A ringfort (TS052-051----) lies 100m to the SSE. Depicted as a standing stone on the 1st (1840) ed. OS 6-inch map. A limestone standing stone (0.52m x 0.17m; H 1.84m), rectangular in plan and orientated ENE-WSW. The top of the stone slopes slightly upwards towards the ENE. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. One of a group of three intervisible standing stones, with TS052-073---- 370m to the NE and TS052-072---- 520m to the N.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS052-072----:
On a slight rise in undulating wet grassland. There are good views in all directions. A rectangular limestone standing stone (0.55m x 0.12m; H 1.2m) orientated NNW-SSE, with evidence of packing stones around the base. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. According to the local landowner this stone was use as a marker to indicate the line of a mass path to a medieval church (TS052-035----) and graveyard (TS052-035001-). One of a group of three intervisible standing stones, TS052-073---- 388m to the SE and TS052-050---- 520m to the S.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS052-073----:
On flat grassland with good views in all directions. A limestone upright (dims.0.3m x 0.12m; H 1.18m) orientated on its long axis NE-SW with a tapering tope which slope from NE up to SW, evidence of packing stones around the base of the upright and the stone is set within a hollow which has been caused by cattle erosion. Now used as a cattle scratching post. According to the local landowner this stone was use as a marker to indicated the line of a mass path to a medieval church (TS052-035----) and graveyard (TS052-035001-). One of a group of three standing stones, standing stone (TS052-072----) visible 388m to the NW and standing stone (TS052-050----) visible 370m to the SW.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS053-016002-:
Collapsed standing stone situated 50m SE of a bowl-barrow (TS053-016001-) atop a NW-SE ridge, in pasture. There are extensive views in all directions. A long recumbent limestone pillar (L 3.05m; 0.5m x 0.47m), rectangular in plan, lying N-S with a sloping top.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS054-011001-:
In grassland on high ground with panoramic views in all directions, nearby ringfort (TS054-012001-) 45m to the E. Stone circle on top of Quinlan's Hill which was recorded in 1938 and has subsequently been levelled. Monument in grassland with so evidence of stone circle or associated enclosure or platform (TS054-011002-) visible. Monument described in 1938 as a stone circle consisting of seven upright stones enclosing a circular area (int. diam. 10m N-S; 27m E-W) with an upright stone (diam. 6ft [1.8m]) in the centre of the circle. Not visible at ground level.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS054-104----:
In undulating pasture, c. 65m E of a motte and bailey (TS054-050003-). A possible limestone standing stone (0.3m x 0.2m; H 1.16m), sub-rectangular in plan and orientated N-S. The stone is quite narrow with a flat top which suggests that it may have been erected as a cattle scratching post. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS055-087----:
On a low NE-SW running ridge, overlooking a small dry valley to the immediate NW, in rough undulating pasture. A limestone standing stone (0.4m x 0.3m; H 1.7m) rectangular in plan and orientated NE-SW. The stone leans to the SW. It tapers to a sharp point at its apex and has an uneven surface covered with white and yellow lichens. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS057-015001-:
In a locally prominent position on top of a broad gently sloping rise in gently undulating pasture on the summit of the external bank of a bowl-barrow (TS057-015001-). There are excellent views in all directions. A sandstone standing stone (0.85m x 0. 35m; H 1m) rectangular in plan and orientated NW-SE. The stone leans to the SW. Packing stones are visible on the SW side of the base. The surface of the stone is weathered.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS057-035----:
On the NE side of a small gently sloping hillock, on a slight NE-facing slope, in undulating pasture. A limestone standing stone (0.7m x 0.26m; H 1.65m) roughly rectangular in plan, orientated N-S. The stone tapers inward slightly from base to top. The surface of the stone is weathered.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS058-023004-:
On top of a bowl-barrow (TS058-023004-) at the centre of an enclosure (TS058-023002-) containing a multi-period complex consisting of two ditch-barrows (TS058-023005- and TS058-023007-), a ring-barrow (TS058-023006-) and a habitation site (TS058-023001-). The complex is located atop the level summit of a prominent hill with panoramic views in all directions. A standing stone (TS058-079----) is visible 800m to the NE; a large barrow 1.5km to the WSW and a mound-barrow (TS058-047----) 1.8km to the S. The stone is perfectly vertical and appears to have been recently re-set as the base is encased in concrete. The standing stone was broken in two during a storm c. 1960s and subsequently repaired by the OPW (Danaher 1973 - excavations.ie). The standing stone consists of a roughly rectangular upright pillar of very fine-grained sandstone (Wth NW-SE at base 0.5m; L at base NE-SW 0.85m; H 2.15m). The stone is roughly rectangular in section. The stone is solidly set in a modern concrete base (Wth NW-SE at base 0.8m; L at base NE-SW 1.2m) with a metal rail (H 0.7m). The surface of the stone is weathered.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS058-079----:
On a slight NW-facing slope on the NW side of a small gently sloping hillock, in undulating pasture. The standing stone (TS058-023004-) at Longstone Hill is visible 800m to the SW. A fine-grained sandstone standing stone (W0.38m x 0.33m; H 1.15m), rectangular in plan. It is solidly set with no packing stones visible. The upper portion of the stone tapers to a point. The surface of the stone is weathered.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS059-058----:
In improved undulating pasture, on a high area of ground. It is named 'Cloghglass' on both the 1840 and 1904 edition OS 6-inch map. Enclosures (TS059-057---- and TS059-059----) are c. 90m to the NE and c. 90m to the SE respectively. The original location of the stone has been quarried, leaving an oval depression (dims. 20m NE-SW; 12m NE-SW; D 1.4m). The limestone standing stone (L 1.15m; 0.7m x 0.5m), now lying prostrate, is located on the N slope of this depression. It tapers towards the top (0.45m x 0.3). The stone is quite weathered, the three exposed faces are generally flat with natural vertical fissures.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS059-096----:
In improved pasture, on a gentle WSW-facing slope. Upstanding stone of limestone (H 1.2m; Wth 0.4m; T 0.25-0.35m) is trapezoidal in plan; long-axis ESE-WNW. Roughly rectangular in elevations and reaches a rounded apex. Hollow around base due to trampling by livestock which use this as a scratching post. Five short parallel scores on NNE elevation may be from sharpening. Monument is located on a low, linear bank (Wth 2m; long-axis NE-SW) flanked by a linear depression on either side which may be a former field boundary. A standing stone (TS067-127----) is located c. 280m to the S.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS059-149----:
In improved pasture, on a high, natural ridge (long axis c. N-S). Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. An upright limestone standing stone (H 1.2m) is square in plan (Wth 0.3m; T 0.25m) with rounded top. It tilts gently to the ENE. Packing stone to N (L 0.3m; Wth 0.15m; T 0.13m) and S (L 0.45m; Wth 0.35m; T 0.17m). Evidence of rubbing by animals and the ground around the base is denuded and poached. According to local information, this stone has always been here in living memory.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-150----:
In improved pasture, on an E-facing slope. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. An upright limestone standing stone (H 1.18m) is rectangular (Wth 0.45m; T 0.18m) in plan; long axis N-S. The top is generally flat. Area around base is hollow due to trampling by livestock. An enclosure (TS059-069----) is c. 10m to W.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-157----:
In improved pasture, on a gentle NW-facing slope. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A limestone standing stone (L 1.6m) leans heavily to the N and is currently H 0.9m above ground level; present long-axis NNW-SSE. It is rectangular in plan (basal Wth 0.48m; top Wth 0.3m; basal T 0.15m; top T 0.09m) and elevation and top slopes upwards to NNW. Hollow around base is likely due to erosion by livestock whilst using stone as scratching post. The field boundary (long axis ENE-WSW) to the N has been removed. Enclosure (TS059-072----) is c. 120m to SW.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-160----:
On a SE-facing slope of an ENE-WSW running ridge, in pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A limestone standing stone (0.35m x 0.25m; H 1.23m) rectangular in plan and orientated NE-SW. It tapers to a point at the top. The standing stone has a rough surface, except where it has been abraded by cattle and there is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. An enclosure (TS059-126----) and a possible standing stone (TS059-161----) are located c. 80m to the S and c. 150m to the W respectively.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-161----:
On a NW-facing slope, in pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A limestone standing stone (0.4m x 0.3m; H 1.3m), rectangular in plan and orientated NE-SW.  It tapers at the top to a point. The standing stone has a rough surface, except where it has been abraded by cattle and there is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. An enclosure (TS059-126----) and a standing stone (TS059-160----) are located c. 110m to the S and c. 150m to the E respectively.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-162----:
In improved level pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A limestone standing stone (0.3m x 0.25m; H 1.5m), regular in plan, with no obvious orientation. It is wider at the base and tapers toward the top which is flat. There is an E-W running field boundary c. 19m to the N and a N-S running tertiary road is c. 26m to the E.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-163----:
In improved pasture, on a NE-facing slope. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. An upright limestone standing stone (0.38m x  0.17m; H 1.25m), rectangular in plan, and orientated E-W. It is sub-rectangular in elevation with natural fissures, particularly on the W elevation. The S elevation has a very rough surface and the stone is flat on top. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion and there is evidence of cattle rubbing on the angles of the stone.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS059-165----:
In lush pasture, on a low rise, with land falling gently to E toward stream. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. An upright limestone standing stone (H 1.05m), rectangular in plan (T max. 0.23m; L max. 0.3m) with its long-axis N-S. The E elevation is convex and the S, W and N elevations are vertical. The ground around the base has been eroded by cattle whilst using the stone as a scratching post. The top of the stone tapers toward the apex. A field boundary to the S (long-axis WNW-ESE) has been removed.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 24 October 2013
TS060-076----:
In level pasture. A limestone standing stone (H0.88m x 0.55m; H 2.1m), rectangular in plan and orientated NNW-SSE, with Galtee Mountains to the SSE. It leans slightly to the W. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion and there is evidence of cattle rubbing on the angles of the stone.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS060-119----:
On a SE-facing slope just below the crest of a hillock in undulating terrain, in tillage. Standing stone has been removed and is currently located in the Cashel Folk Museum (see TS061-146----). There is a slight hollow (diam. c. 12m) immediately below the crest of a hillock which seems the likely location of the standing stone. According to the landowner the stone was removed c. 20 years ago as a result of field clearance. This monument is indicated on the 1st (1840) ed. OS 6-inch map but is not depicted on the 2nd (1906) ed.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS061-152----:
In a slight hollow, in improved pasture on a NW-facing slope with excellent views W-NE across the plains of Cashel. An upright limestone orthostat (H 2m), rectangular in plan (L 0.28m; Wth 0.25m) with no obvious orientation, although it leans distinctively downslope to NW. The stone narrows toward the top and is split towards the top of the NE face where it has fractured. There is evidence of cattle rubbing on the NW face and on the angles. (O'Brien 2006, 16-17).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS061-153----:
On a NW-facing slope, in a dip in the landscape between Palmer's Hill to the SW and Ballyknock Hill to the NE, in improved pasture. There are good views over the plains of Cashel to the NW. An upright limestone standing stone (0.4m x 0.27m; H 1.3m), rectangular in plan and orientated ENE-WSW. The stone leans towards the SSE and all faces have evidence of cattle wearing. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. (O'Brien 2006, 16-17).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS061-154----:
On a SE-facing slope of Ballyknock Hill, in improved pasture. There are good views from E-NW. An upright limestone stone (0.48m x 0.41; H 1.52m), rectangular in plan and orientated ENE-WSW. It leans to the NNE. There is one large packing stone and others may be obscured by grass tufts. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. O'Brien (2006, 16-17) describes a number of stones protruding from the ground immediately N of the standing stone as possible packing stones or a possible cist (0.4m x 0.5m) formed by two short side stones and lone long stone, with the base of the standing stone forming the back.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS062-068----:
In fallow tillage, on a NW-facing slope 270m below the summit of Knockapharson hill and just above a 500ft contour. There are excellent views from W-N-E. According to local information, 'Cloghleigh' is a substantial natural boulder c. 10 tonnes in weight. It was moved in recent years downslope to the NE, into the W end of a grove of cypress trees where it currently rests, overgrown with briars. On both the 1st (1840) and 1903-04 ed. OS 6-inch map the stone is depicted immediately E of a field boundary running NE-SW which, together with the stone, has since been removed. The field where the stone stood is known locally as the 'The Rock Field'. It is likely that 'Cloghleigh' refers to a natural boulder and not a standing stone.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS062-154----:
In improved pasture, in a gentle hollow (diam. c. 2.5m), on a S-facing slope. Enclosures (TS062-105---- and TS062-155----) are located c. 30m to SSW and c. 90m to NNW respectively. A limestone standing stone (0.35m x 0.25m; H 1.35m) rectangular in plan and orientated NW-SE. The stone leans gently to the SW. There is evidence of cattle wear on the angles of the stone and lichens are growing on its surface.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS066-069----:
On a SE-facing slope, in improved pasture. Depicted and named 'Legaun' on the 1904 ed. OS 6-inch map. The stone is not longer at this location, however, there is a depression (diam. 1.4m; D 0.2m) where the area around the base of the stone has been eroded by cattle. A recumbent limestone stone (L c. 2m; c. 0.3m x c. 0.2m), which tapers at one end, lies against base of a ENE-WSW running field boundary c. 30m to the N. It is likely that this is the standing stone. The field boundaries E of the standing stone have been removed.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS066-181----:
In rough, level pasture to the SE of old farm buildings. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A standing stone (0.45m x 0.25m; H 1.65m), rectangular in plan and orientated ESE-WNW. It is tilting slightly to the SSW. The stone rises to a subtle point at the apex. There is a slight depression around the base at the SSW caused by cattle erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 9 September 2014
TS066-185----:
In a level area of gently undulating pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A limestone standing stone (0.51m x 0.22m; H 1.2m), rectangular in plan and orientated NNW-SSE. It has a flat, rectangular top which slopes gently downwards to the NNW. There is a farm access roadway c. 19m to the E.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 9 September 2014
TS066-186----:
On a level area near the top of a SE-facing slope, in improved pasture. Identified during ASI fieldwork. An enclosure (TS066-170----) is located c. 32m to the NE. A standing stone (0.48m x 0.14m; H 1.65m), rectangular in plan and orientated NNW-SSE, possibly aligned with a peak in the Galtee Mountains to the SSE. The stone has a wedge-shaped point at its apex. Raised spots on the western elevation appear to be natural and notches at the SE angle appear man-made. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 9 September 2014
TS066-198----:
Slightly off the summit of a hillock in gently undulating terrain, under pasture. Identified during field survey. There is a ditch barrow (TS066-166----) 86m to the NNW, a ring-barrow (TS066-172----) and stepped barrow (TS066-122----) 100m and 180m to the S respectively. An upright of sedimentary stone (dims. at base 0.47m; at top 0.43m NE-SW x 0.16m NW-SE; H 1.83m) of rectangular section and orientated ENE-WSW (60°-240°). The stone tapers slightly towards the top and the apex of the stone slopes upwards towards the WSW. Due to the sedimentary nature of the stone the sides are very flat and straight. There is a hollow depression (D 0.25-03m; Wth 4.5-4.7m) around the base of the stone caused by cattle poaching when they use the stone as a scratching post.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 9 September 2014
TS066-202----:
On a gradual SE-facing slope of a hill, in undulating terrain, under pasture. According to the landowner the standing stone had fallen over and he re-erected it though it may not be in the exact location or on the original orientation. He described packing stones at the base of the standing stone when it fall over. A deep slurry pond has been excavated immediately W of the standing stone and there is a large shed 4.6m to the N. There are good views to E, Galtees visible to the S and Slievenamuck mountain dominating the view to the SW. The view N is impeded by the rising slope. A red sandstone standing stone (H 1.38m; 0.64m x 0.46m), with very few inclusions. There are some small quartz pebbles visible at the SE side of the E face. The stone is currently aligned N-S along its long axis. It is rectangular in plan, tapering towards the top to a point, though this is partially the result of spalling. The outer surface of the lower portion of the E face is badly spawled.

Compiled by: Jean Farrelly

TS067-011007-:
Indicated on the 1st (1840) and 2nd (1954) ed. 6-inch OS map as 'Coirthe Tlachtgha' in the N portion of a graveyard (TS067-011006-) associated with the medieval church of Corroge (TS067-067011004-). In Dinneen's dictionary (1927) 'Coirthe' means a stone, particularly a memorial stone and 'Tlachtgha' means 'a seat of early rights'. In the 1970s the graveyard was incorporated into the adjacent quarry and at that time the standing stone was broken and pushed into the SE edge of the graveyard.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly

TS067-119----:
On a steep N-facing slope, in pasture. Upright conglomerate stone (1.25m x 0.75m; H 1.65m), rectangular in plan and oriented NW-SE. There are small packing stones around base. An enclosure (TS067-068----) lies c. 185m to the NW.

TS067-127----:
In improved pasture, rough and poorly drained in places, situated on a higher part of the field. A standing stone (TS059-096----) is located c. 280m to the N. TS067-129----:

Indicated as a rock or outcrop in the River Suir, adjacent to the N bank, on the 1st (1840) and 1900-05 ed. TS071-011004-:
On the crest of a hill in undulating terrain, in grassland. There are very good views in all directions with Slievenamon Mountain dominating from ESE-S. Standing stone of red sandstone (L 2.61m; 0.6m x 0.3m) which is lying prostrate where it appears to have collapsed. The stone has split into two, the upper portion (L 1.53m; 0.6m x 0.30m) tapers towards the top (0.21m x 0.21m). The lower portion (L 1.08m; 0.62m x 0.31m) is fairly consistent in width and thickness. Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 29 September 2014
TS071-017001-:
On an ESE-facing slope, off-centre to S within the interior of an enclosure (TS071-017----), in pasture . Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A conglomerate standing stone (1.1m x 0.8m; H 1.2m) irregular in plan and orientated NE-SW. It is squat and rises to a flat point. There is a depression around the NE and SE base of the stone due to cattle erosion. According to local information, a second stone was removed from beside the ditch in the field adjacent to W. There is a standing stone (TS071-055----) located c. 45m to the W and another (TS071-056----) c. 260m to the SW.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS071-054----:
In upland heath, on a SE-facing slope of Sheegouna, on the eastern side of Slievenamon Mountain. Monument identified during field survey. A rectangular structure (overall dims. 2.8m N-S; 2.5m E-W; internal dims. 2.25m E-W; 1.1m N-S tapering to 0.6m towards the rear) which opens out to the E. The side walls are constructed of a combination of orthostats (H 0.77-1.1m) and rubble stone wall (T 0.8m) and are leaning into the interior. There is one lintel (dims. L 0.92m; T c. 0.4m) towards the rear supported on two orthostats and another collapsed stone (L 0.75m; T 0.36m) at the rear which appears to have been another lintel. The entrance is defined on either side by orthostats. A wall (int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.6m) runs from the entrance northwards, revetting the hillslope. Cairn (TS071-021----) on Sheegouna is c. 112m to NE. The passage tombs at Knockroe (KK034-019001-) and Baunfree (KK034-031----), Co. Kilkenny are located 10km to the E and 13KM to ENE respectively. A small triangular-shaped stone (H 0.35m; T 0.42m) is located 18m to the WSW and is similar to the triangular-shaped stone associated with the nearby cairn (TS071-021----).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 30 September 2014
TS071-055----:
On an ESE-facing slope, in pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. Standing stone of sandstone and quartz conglomerate with some pebbles on the E side (1m x 0.5m; H 0.8m), rectangular in plan and orientated NNW-SSE. There is a packing stone at base on W side. The angles of the stone are worn from cattle abrasion. According to local information, a second stone was removed recently from beside the ditch to the E. A standing stone (TS071-017001-) and enclosure (TS071-017----) are located c. 45m to the E and another standing stone (TS071-056----) is c. 220m to the WSW.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 30 September 2014
TS071-056----:
On a SE-facing slope, in pasture. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A standing stone of sandstone conglomerate with quartz pebbles (1.15m x 0.5m; H 1.0m) sub-rectangular in plan and orientated N-S. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion. A standing stone (TS071-017001-) and enclosure (TS071-017----) are located c. 260m to the ENE and another standing stone (TS071-055----) is c. 220m to the ENE.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of revised upload: 30 September 2014
TS072-009----:
On a gentle WSW-facing slope, overlooking the valley of the Lingaun River to the SW, in pasture. A cairn (TS078-001----) is visible on Slievenamon c. 7km due W. An upright stone (1.65m x 0.55m; H 2.6m) of red sandstone, orientated NE-SW and tapering to a point. The stone is sub-rectangular in plan with natural cleavage plains and sub-circular depressions on the NW and SW sides. There are possible packing stones at the base. According to Power (1908, 200) the stone was incorporated into field fence. This field fence has subsequently been removed.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS073-006----:
On a platform in gently sloping moorland on the W slope of Moanour mountain which is at the W end of Slievenamuck mountain. This wedge-tomb is partially buried in the surrounding bog. It consists of a long wedge-shaped gallery (L 5.4m; Wth 1.1m tapering to 0.65m at the backstone), flanked at either side by the remains of an outer wall (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 95-6). A pair of orthostats stand behind the E end of the gallery (ibid.). Two roofstones lie across the middle of the gallery and a displaced roofstone rests above the orthostats at the W end of the N side (ibid.). A number of displaced stones lie in front of the entrance (ibid.). The structure is incorporated in a roughly circular mound (diam. 8-9m) which rises little above the surface of the bog (ibid.). Monument is quite heavily overgrown with gorse, brambles, ferns and scrub with a rowan tree on the S side of the E end growing on the tomb.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
TS073-007----:
On the summit of Shrough Hill, part of the Slievenamuck/Moanour mountains, with forestry encroaching to within 10m to N, E and W, forestry to W has been felled affording an extensive view of the Galty mountains and foothills below. A cairn, possibly a passage tomb (LI058-001----), is visible on Temple Hill c. 9km to the SSE, at the W end of the Galtys. A stone wall runs E-W along the S edge of the mound. The monument consists of a roughly circular cairn (diam. 30m; H 2m) with a small, roofless polyogonal chamber (int. dims. L 2.2m; Wth 1.2m), aligned roughly E-W, near the centre of the cairn (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1982, 101; Ó Nualláin and Cody 1987, 76-8). The sidestones vary in height from 1.2m to 1.8m (ibid. 76). The cairn is overgrown with gorse, heather and low scrub.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume IV. Counties Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1982)
TS073-033----:
On a gentle SW-facing slope in undulating upland terrain. A field boundary which ran N-S immediately E of the standing stone has been cleared and the field reclaimed. A red sandstone conglomerate, rectangular in plan (dims. L 0.95m; Wth 0.47m; H 1.26m) and aligned NNW-SSE. It stands in a hollow caused by cattle poaching. There are no visible packing stones around base which has a grassy hummock at the SE end and a low hummock along the E side. The upper portion of the NE face has spawled creating a slight ledge across this face.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS074-024----:
On the NE edge of a small natural flat-topped hillock on a gentle N-facing slope, in pasture in the Glen of Aherlow. A tributary of the River Aherlow flows roughly N-S 30m to the W. There are good views in all directions with a range of hills, including Slievenamuck, visible to the N, while the view ESE-S-W is dominated by the Galtees. This standing stone (0.53m x 0.42m; H 1.1m), composed of red sandstone conglomerate with quartz inclusions protruding, is rectangular in plan and orientated NE-SW. The NE and NW sides bulge out as the stone rises while the other faces are quite flat. The stone appears to be leaning towards the N.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 29 July 2013
TS075-039----:
Enclosing a hilltop with a steep drop to the SW and a more gradual fall of slope to the NE before the ground levels out within the NE quadrant. Ringfort (TS075-040----) located c. 50m to the NE. The summit of the hill runs NW-SE roughly through the centre of the monument. Large steep-sided hillock (diam. 170m N-S and E-W) enclosed by internal fosse (Wth 3.4m) and large substantial outer bank (Wth crest 6-10.5m; base 8.7-14m; int. H 2.3-2.78m; ext. H 1.17-3.6m). A modern stone wall has been built on portion of the bank in the NE quadrant from N to NE. The summit has been partially quarried into resulting in an irregular hollow N of centre. There is a cattle gap through the bank in the WSW. There is a lot of stone evident in the grass-covered bank. The bank in the S quadrant has been quarried into and the bank in the SE is slightly denuded. From E-SE the bank has been levelled with only low traces surviving. In the NW sector the bank kinks out to form a possible structure (dims. 10.3m NE-SW; 12m NW-SE) or may be result of quarrying. There is a possible entrance (Wth 2m) to the enclosure immediately W of this structure. The OS Letters refer to some interference with the bank at the NE and S sides where 'lately part of it was pared off outwardly...for a byroad that runs here now' (O'Flanagan 1930, vol. 2, 125).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 7 April 2014
TS075-045----:
On the break of a S-facing slope of Bain at the eastern end of the Galty mountains, in forestry. Deciduous scrub and ferns are reclaiming the slope after previous vegetation was burnt. Extensive view to E and S but blocked upslope to N and by trees to W. Possible portal tomb (per. comm. Paul Walsh 1991) consisting of a large sandstone conglomerate slab (dims. 2.8m x 2.94m) partially resting on a triangular-shaped side-stone (H 0.91m ext., 1.23m int.; max. L 1.07m; T 0.28m) to the SW, sloping down to the NE where it rests on the ground. Aligned NW-SE presuming that the triangular stone is a side-stone. A distinct linear depression (Wth 0.23-0.32m; D 0.02-0.08m) runs NE-SW across the centre of the capstone. There is a lot of stone rubble in the chamber. There is a rectangular block of quartz (dims. 0.22m x 0.36m) lying loose immediately NE of tomb and a scatter of rubble extends c. 3m SW of the tomb. There is also a mound of rubble (dims. c. 3.5m x 2.5m; H 1.2m) 1.5m to N.

Date of upload: 25 June 2015
TS076-038----:
Formerly on a natural flat ridge, in undulating pasture. There are extensive views in all directions. A standing stone is indicated as 'leagaun' on the 1901-05 ed. OS 6-inch map. In flat terrain with large sand pit c. 20m to S, in undulating terrain under pasture. There are very good views from SE-S-W, but limited to the N to NE by Curraghdobbin and Carrigadoon hills. TS078-074----:
On a gentle N-NW-facing slope in undulating terrain, under pasture. There are good views to the N but poor uphill to the E and S and limited to the W. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. Grey sandstone conglomerate with quartz pebble inclusions (0.72m x 0.4m; H 1.74m) roughly rectangular in plan and tapering towards the top. It is orientated N-S, with broad faces to the E and W. The top of the stone slopes, rising to the N. There are packing stones around the base.

Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS078-075----:
On a gradual SE-facing slope in undulating terrain, in pasture. Top of cairn (TS078-001----) on Slievenamon just visible on crest of mountain. Grey sandstone conglomerate, aligned NE-SW. Rectangular in plan (L 0.47m; Wth 0.33m; H 1.34m). It is weathered giving a slightly rounded appearance to the angles. The top of the stone slopes, rising to the SW.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS078-078----:
On the E mountain slope of Slievenamon. A cairn (TS078-001----) is situated just E of the summit of the mountain and is 150m WNW of the cursus. Another cairn (TS071-021----) is visible 1km to N from the upper end of the cursus and an unclassified megalithic tomb (TS071-064----), though not visible, is located c. 930m to the N. The view NE-E-S is extensive, with the passage tomb at Knockroe (KK034-019001-) c. 10km to the E and the passage tomb at Baunfree (KK034-031----) c. 13km to the SE. Aligned roughly E-W, the monument, running downslope, consists of two roughly parallel stone banks (N bank Wth 1.9m at top; overall Wth 3.3m; H 0.3m; S bank Wth 1.3m at top; overall Wth 2.2-2.9m; H 0.25-0.35m) overgrowth with grass, moss and heather. The banks are 90m apart, though they narrow to 75m at the upper western end. The upper end terminates with a bank (Wth 2.7m at top; overall Wth 5.5m; int. H 1m; ext. H 0.22m) which curves at the NW angle, while at the SW angle there is a gap (Wth 2.7m). The N bank runs E-W from the W end for 118m before turning ESE for the remaining c. 260m while the S bank runs ESE-WNW for its entire length of c. 360m. The upper end of the monument is on a relatively gentle slope, however, the ground level becomes increasingly steeper and both banks appear to terminate at the E end where the ground level becomes very steep. Similar cursus monuments have been identified in Carlow (CW020-026----; CW020-027----); Kilkenny (KK005-004----); Kildare (KD032-058----) and Wicklow (WI005-124----; WI027-089----).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 23 May 2016
TS078-079----:
In upland area, on a lower SE slope of Slievenamon Mountain, in pasture. Extensive view E and S with the Comeragh Mountains in the distance from S-SW. A large red sandstone boulder with some pebble inclusions, aligned E-W. Roughly rectangular in plan (L 1.37m x Wth 0.52m; H 1.4m) with broad faces to the N and S, it narrows slightly as it rises (Wth 0.2-0.48m). Some fractures evident. N face is very irregular, having suffered much spawling. The ground around the base of stone has been poached by cattle, creating a hollow. The stone rises slightly higher at the W end, but this may be a result of how the stone has fractured and broken. There is a thin seam of quartz towards the base at the E end of the S face.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 14 November 2016
TS079-047----:
On level ground in the Clasha river valley with good views in all directions. The Comeragh Mountains are visible to the SW. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A sandstone standing stone with some quartz inclusions (0.62m x 0.44; H 1.45m) rectangular in plan and orientated E-W. There is a depression around the base of the stone due to cattle erosion.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS079-048----:
On flat ground with Carrigadoon Hill rising to the S, in pasture. There are extensive views to the E and good to the W. The field is known locally as 'Parc na clocha'. A sandstone standing stone (max 1m x 0.58m; H 1.9m) rectangular in plan and orientated E-W. It is fractured at the base into two stones. The larger stone (1m x 0.36m; H 1.9m) leans to the N  and is vertically cracked down its full length. The smaller stone (0.9m x 0.26m; H 0.95m) stands to the S and is broken vertically down its full length. Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS079-049----:
On flat ground in gently undulating terrain, in pasture. There are good views in all directions. A standing stone (0.55m x 0.52m; H 2m), rectangular in plan, was lying prostrate at this position before it was moved c. 20 years ago (c. 1980) c. 300m S and placed in an upright position in the front garden of a bungalow (see TS079-050----). A large circular enclosure (TS079-051----) lies c. 85m to the E.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011

On a SE-facing slope in the Galtee Mountains, overlooking an extensive plain and mountains beyond to the SE, otherwise surrounded by mountain slopes. The stone tapers towards the top (0.67m x 0.24m). Though relatively low, this standing stone is prominent on the open mountains slopes.

On the NE edge of a gentle N-facing ridge, in pasture. TS083-021006-:
Near the N edge of a roughly E-W running ridge, c. 60m S of the River Suir which runs parallel to the ridge, in pasture. There is a field boundary immediately E of the standing stone with a factory complex on the other side to the E. A sandstone standing stone (max. 0.38m x 0.26m; H 1.23m) rectangular in plan and orientated NNE-SSW. The stone tapers to a point. It is broadest in the middle and narrows to a rectangular base (0.29m x 0.23m). The surface is spawled, though both broad faces are fairly flat. There are several large fractures and evidence of where stone has fractured off at the SW and NW angles, towards the base. There is also a bad crack 0.5m above ground level on the S face, the W end of which rises up through the stone. There are some grass clumps around the base of the stone but no evidence of any packing stones.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 12 November 2013
TS083-034----:
Identified during construction work for a housing development on the NE outskirts of Clonmel (Elder 2003, 381). On a slight rise and c. 750m N of the River Suir. According to Elder (ibid.) the standing stone (0.43m x 0.19m; H 1.25m), rectangular in plan, appears to be of quarried granite and partially dressed. Elder (ibid.) noted on the NW angle 'traces of a possible ogham inscription, although this is quite weathered and difficult to determine'. He also noted that, 'it is likely that the stone was transported by a former landowner from an as yet unknown location, but possibly a nearby enclosure site, (TS083-023----)' (ibid.). The stone was removed and its current location is unknown. If the stone is composed of dressed granite then it is likely to be a scratching post erected in the 19th or 20th century.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 March 2020
TS088-033002-:
On a slight natural rise on a NE-facing slope, within the SE quadrant of a triangular-shaped graveyard (TS088-033001-), in rough hummocky pasture. The view to the E is extensive, good to the N and S and impeded upslope to the W. An old red sandstone standing stone (0.5m x 0.3m; H 0.8m) trapezoidal in plan and orientated E-W. It narrows towards the top, which has a flat surface (0.52m x 0.18m). According to Power (1908, 45-78) this is the location of an early church site (TS088-033----).
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 02 December 2013
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 4/1997).
TS088-069----:
On a steep N-facing slope in upland terrain, in rough pasture. A stream runs roughly N-S c. 80m to the E. There are extensive views to the N and W, but limited to the E and S. A standing stone (0.62m x 0.3m; H 0.94m), roughly rectangular in plan, orientated NE-SW. Composed of red sandstone, the SE and NW faces are flat, though the latter has fractured due to weathering. It is flat-topped (0.44m x 0.24m). There is a large slab of bedrock (1.3m x 0.3m; H 0.35m) exposed at the foot of the NW face of the stone. There are several stones around the base of the SW and NW sides, possibly packing stones.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 05 December 2013
TS088-070----:
On a N-facing slope, just off the flat crest of a ridge, at the foot of Knockperry South hill. There are extensive views to the N and W, good to the E and impeded to the S. Large red sandstone standing stone (L 2.37m; 1.1m x 0.5m) rectangular in plan. It is known locally as 'the Bishop' because it narrows towards the top (0.7m x 0.44m) giving the appearance of a head on a larger body. This narrowing appears to be due to weathering, where the stone has cracked and broken off. The stone had fallen over, with the base facing S, and was subsequently re-erected (H 2.12m above ground), giving an orientation NW-SE. There are packing stones at the base on the SE side.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 6 December 2013
TS088-077----:
Toward the E end of the summit of a flat-topped hill in undulating terrain. There are extensive views in all directions. A sandstone standing stone (0.87m x 0.3m; H 1.76m) roughly rectangular in plan and orientated E-W, rising to a point at the E end. The standing stone tapers as it rises and leans to the NW. There is a lot of limestone outcrop on the summit of the hill and there is a stone at the NW base and another near the NE base (c. 0.4-0.6m) as well as some smaller stones which may be packing stones.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS091-004----:
On broad, flat break of a NW-facing, gently undulating, slope. In upland terrain, under pasture. This stone pair consists of a large, flat-topped pillar stone and a smaller stone lying 1.95m to E which has a triangular profile and sloping top. Both stones are composed of red sandstone with quartz inclusions. Both stones are aligned SW-NE (front face to SW). The upright stone has a distinctive vertical quartz vein with a smaller one on the NE side and is rectangular in plan (Wth 0.5m NE; 0.59m SW; 0.61m SW; 0.8m NW) with a number of packing stones. The prostrate stone is five-sided (Wth 0.5m NE; 0.54m SE; 0.28m S; 0.43m SW; 0.63m NW) with a packing stone on its NW side. A small boulder (O.56m x 0.3m) lies between the two standing stones but is not embedded. Four small cairns (TS091-004001-), possibly prehistoric field clearance cairns, are located to NW and N of standing stones.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS091-005----:
On the break of an E-facing slope in upland terrain, under pasture. Stone pair aligned NE (50 degrees)-SW (230 degrees). Lower stone(max. H 0.97m) at the NE end of the alignment has a rounded profile and leans to SE. It is composed of reddish sandstone with quartz veins and has an irregular rectangular plan (Wth 0.5m NE; 0.8m SE; 0.64m SW; 1.12m NW). The taller stone (H 1.93), lies 1.3m to SW. It is composed of a darker red sandstone and has a number of packing stones around its base. It is roughly square in plan (Wth 0.55m NE; 0.6m SE; 0.64m SW; 0.55m NW), though it broadens out towards its flat top (Wth 0.69m NW). This stone is badly spawled, however, there is a suggestion of ogham script on the S angle, with two incisded horizontal lines 0.44m from the top and 0.03m apart. There are a number of loose stones lying about, possibly clearance. Slight hollow at base of both stones probably result of cattle scratching.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS091-018----:
On a N-facing slope of Knockperry South hill, in rough upland pasture. There are good views in all directions except to the S. Monument identified during ASI fieldwork. A red sandstone standing stone (0.6m x 0.4m; H 2m) lozenge-shaped in plan and orientated NE-SW. The stone, which is quite badly spawled, rises to an apex towards the SW. There are some hummocks at the base of the stone, with some stones on SE side which may be packing stones.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 26 August 2011
TS091-020----:
On a S-facing slope of Knocknagearagh hill in the Knockmealdown Mountains, in fairly level upland terrain, under rough pasture. A sandstone standing stone, roughly rectangular in plan (L 0.66m x Wth 0.3m; H 1.03m) orientated N-S with a peak rising to the N. There are no packing stones visible but the base is obscured by a grassy hummock. The E face is fractured.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 03 March 2014
TS091A002----:
At the base of an E-facing slope in a small river valley of Aughavanlomaun Stream which runs NW-SE. Views from this standing stone are limited by rising hills to the N and S, though a stone pair (TS091-005----) is visible on top of the hill to the S. This is a sandstone conglomerate (0-8m x 0.3-0.65m; H 1.1m). It appears to be orientated E-W, though the long axis is N-S. It is irregular in plan, narrowing towards the S end. There is a small stone at the base on the W side. The stone is leaning towards the W and the top surface rises to a peak towards the E.
Compiled by: Jean Farrelly
Date of upload: 10 May 2012
